newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. comptroller confident Troy will solve impasse.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. comptroller confident Troy will solve impasse.

text.p: Troy, N.Y., is still at risk of defaulting on a payment on $35 million of debt that is due on September 15, but the state's financial watchdog on Thursday said he was confident the problem will be solved.

Still, even if the city got the bondholders to accept a late payment of the $1.4 million they are owed, rating agencies said such a deferral would be tantamount to a default. "We consider it a default," said Marcy Block, an assistant vice president at Moody's Investors Service.
And while the city is continuing to negotiate with its bondholders, no progress has been achieved in the past two days, officials from the city and Moody's said.

While the city does not have the funds to make the $1.4 million payment, the director of the office of management and budget for Troy made it plain that it still is possible that the city will reach a speedy agreement with the bondholders.
"We could come to an agreement tomorrow," said Owen Goldfarb, adding that whether the city would default was "pure speculation."

The issues dividing the two sides include a clash over whether the Municipal Assistance Corp (MAC), which the state imposed in 1995 due to the Troy's poor financial condition, would issue new debt to repay the bondholders, Block said.
Alternatively, new MAC debt might be substituted for the $35 million of debt that was issued by the local Industrial Development Agency under a lease back mortgage arrangement.

Troy, which has been paying a fairly high interest rate of 8.8 percent on this issue also wants to refinance it at lower rates, but the city and the bondholders have yet to agree on what would be an acceptable rate, she said. The structure of the new debt is another issue.

The city, whose debt service totaled more than $9 million, or 25 percent of its annual expenses in January 1996, will get $9.1 million of aid from the state in fiscal 1997, when all sources are counted, including an accelerated payment.

Whether the comptroller, who in late 1994 bought the city's bond anticipation notes for a short-term pool because Troy was unable to sell the debt on its own, will provide any further assistance is not yet known.

"The city is still working with the bondholders to try to come up with an acceptable solution, and we're confident they will," said Dennis Tompkins, a spokesman for the comptroller, H. Carl McCall. The spokesman added the comptroller's staff were monitoring Troy's difficulties.
McCall last month was forced to help Utica, another upstate town whose finances have been battered, avoid a default by buying $2.145 million of notes to help the city complete a refinancing.
